question: What is the meaning of product cost in relation to general details?
description: The meaning of product cost in relation to general details is associated with potential cost reduction enabled by technical/usage data through re-use or remanufacturing.

The ‘Quantity’ pattern makes it possible to specify the 
kind or type of the quantity. For example, ‘Length’, ‘Density’ or ‘Weight’ 
would be different kinds of quantities. The numerical value associated 
with a quantity typically consists of a unit and a number. The ‘Quantity’ 
pattern is well suited to capture these attributes in interoperable and 
scalable manner (see Fig. 5). 
A product may have different types or modification of existing types. 
The ‘Explicit Typing’ pattern is selected to explicitly define types for 
each product (see Fig. 5). 
Products often involve instructions such as assembly, disassembly 
and installation. Instructions might not always be simple strings.

instructions using datatype properties cannot capture additional

• Difficulties to extract material from used products at an equal high 
quality of raw material extraction (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 
2020). 
Component manufacturer  
• Access to new markets because of quality information of material and 
object components (Hansen et al., 2018; Munaro and Tavares, 2021; 
Smeets et al., 2019).  
• Proposition value of CE-based products (or proper mix between new 
and CE-based products) (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Munaro 
and Tavares, 2021).  
• Potential cost reduction (lower testing, reconditioning and fabrication 
costs enabled by technical/usage data) through re-use or remanu­
facturing (Smeets et al., 2019).  
• Uncertain quality of resources (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020; 
Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).  
• Inaccurate spare part or material availability prediction (Malmgren 
and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020; Spengler and Schr¨oter, 2003; Wittenveen 
& Bos, 2018).  
• Lack of standardized components and materials which facilitates 
inter-operable reuse (Honic et al., 2019a).  
• Potential liability issues when materials are reused (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016).  
• Data provision costs (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Firms lack of willingness to be transparent (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Confidentiality issues (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Attitude transition from sell faster and more, towards get paid to 
deliver the most circular product (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 
2020).  
• Adapting to reverse logistics requires searching new CE sourcing 
partners (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020). 
Architect  
• Feedback  
• Life cycle feedback of objects (e.g. material choices) to make better 
product design for circular goals (Kanters, 2020).  
• Understanding the preference/use of an object by the end-user to 
optimize the product design for user experience (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016).  
• Better value proposition  
• Proposition value of CE-based product (Hansen et al., 2018).  
• More accurate valuation of an object (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Covering support for warranty issues (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Standardization improves circularity but limits design freedom for 
architects (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).  
• Data not (yet) available (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Firms lack of willingness to be transparent (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• (passport) Data provision costs (Rudolphi, 2018). 
Contractor (incl. assembler)  
• Better proposition  
• Information availability (e.g., IoT-based maintenance prediction) 
extends life-time of an object and reduces maintenance costs, which 
may be a propositional advantage in long-term licensed-based ser­
vice contracting (Bouwend Nederland, 2020; Chahine, 2021; 
Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Munaro and Tavares, 2021).  
• To improve the residual value and current (CE) performance of 
their buildings (Bouwend Nederland, 2020; Hansen et al., 2018).  
• Data provision costs (do not yet out wage the benefits but are 
expected to do so in the near future as data management cost will 
decrease because (1) it becomes a general practice and (2) 
environmental cost are expected to rise) (Bouwend Nederland, 
2020).  
• Smaller firms typically lack behind in information management and 
will have incurred costs with adopting a passport (Bouwend 
Nederland, 2020).
